## A city that watches back

The cameras were supposed to make the street legible to the state \[@smith2020]. Instead they made the state legible to the street — and the argument of this piece is that the reversal, not the surveillance, is what the city failed to plan for \[@smith2020; @jones2021].

> What the lens records, the record can return.

The program's defenders make three claims. First, that the footage reduced violent crime in the pilot corridor \[@doe2019, p. 12]. Second, that retention limits were honored[^1]. Third — and this is where the piece pushes back — that oversight was meaningful.

### What the ledger shows

- the retention window drifted from 30 to 45 days without a hearing
- the oversight board met twice in eighteen months
- a third of the flagged clips had no case attached

[^1]: The policy text says thirty; the retention reports say forty-five.

## The counterargument, answered

Critics of this reading argue that audit trails are a technicality \[@jones2021]. They are not. The audit trail is the only artifact a court can compel, and the gap between policy and practice lives entirely inside it.

Final words: the injury is real, and it is *shown*, not merely asserted.
